sources.headline: Trump expands hunt for voter fraud ahead of midterms
sources.text: By Elissa FitzgeraldTopic:World PoliticsPosted Thu 29 Oct 2026 at 7:12amThu 29 Oct 2026 at 7:12amSupporter arrive at a rally held by Barack Obama and Democratic senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia. (Reuters: Edgar Su)Hello! Welcome back to our US midterms briefing.Click here to see how popular Trump is today, and click here for a quick breakdown on what the midterms are all about.Here's what you need to know todayPresidents hit the trail: Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former president Barack Obama are heading to Ohio and Georgia respectively to shore up votes as the US enters its last week before the midterms. These states are the sites of critical contests that could decide which party could control the US Senate for the remainder of Trump's term. Obama kept a low profile for most of this election cycle, but has hit the campaign trail in recent days to deliver some fiery speeches against his successor.Hunt for non-citizen voters: The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, Reuters reports. It's the latest in an effort to uncover evidence of voter fraud. Election officials and lawyers worry the investigations could undermine confidence in election systems, and be used to attack the legitimacy of narrow races. Since Trump returned to office, prosecutors have accused at least 147 people of illegally voting, Reuters reports, but the cases amount to fewer than one for every million people who voted in 2024.The tale of two Dans: If you missed it, Republican senator Dan Sullivan is defending his Alaska seat from independent candidate … Dan Sullivan. It's been a point of ire for Republicans for months, with (unsuccessful) challenges to throw the newcomer off the ballot making it all the way to the Alaska Supreme Court. They argue the second Sullivan (AKA, Dan J Sullivan) is running just to confuse voters. Dan J Sullivan has maintained he's running for legitimate reasons. But a New York Times exclusive has put a new twist in the tale, reporting that campaign aides for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola sought a spoiler candidate by the name of Dan Sullivan to undermine the senator back in 2025.A deeper diveI messaged North America correspondent Kamin Gock about the Republican Party's standing in states that are typically conservative. Here's what he had to say.Elissa FitzgeraldTrump is off to Ohio after a campaign blitz in Texas yesterday. That's a lot of time spent on what are usually safe Republican areas. Is he worried about losing ground here?Kamin GockAbsolutely — this will be his third visit to the state this month! Ohio has been reliably Republican in Senate races. But it could now be a crucial battle ground, with polls showing a very competitive race between Republican Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown. If the Democrats pick up four Senate seats across the country, they'll retake control of the upper house. In Ohio, Democrats also hope they can pick up a seat in the House of Representatives and none of that spells good news for Trump.Elissa FitzgeraldYou spent some time in Nebraska — another typically red state — not long ago. What did you learn there?Kamin GockSome farmers are really feeling rising costs linked to tariffs and the Iran war, particularly fuel and fertiliser price hikes. One farmer told me he is paying an extra $US1,400 ($1984) a day for diesel to operate his farm. Those are extra costs the farmers I spoke to say they did not vote for.Kamin GockThere was a lot of disquiet and disappointment among Republicans, but just because they are unhappy with Trump doesn't mean they will vote Democrat. As one man told me, he probably just won't vote.You can read more about Kamin's trip to Nebraska here.How popular is Donald Trump today?US President Donald Trump might not be up for election at the midterms, but his popularity will have a strong influence over the outcome.The president's party almost always loses House seats in midterm elections and that trend gets steeper when the president is unpopular.Historic polling data collated by analytics firm Gallup shows presidents with approval ratings below 50 per cent have seen their party lose an average of 37 House seats.Presidents with approval ratings above 50 per cent have netted smaller loses, with an average of 14 seats.Your crash course on the midtermsClick here to go back to the top.And here's how to stay up to dateYou can keep track of the latest out of the US here.Thanks for joining me! I'll be back same time tomorrow with more.

sources.headline: US Justice Dept loses initial bid to block votes from alleged noncitizens in California
sources.text: Oct 28 - A US judge rejected on Wednesday a request by the Justice Department to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots for the November 3 midterm elections received from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.The decision marks the latest setback for President Donald Trump's effort to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress.US District Judge David Carter issued the decision after a hearing on Tuesday in Los Angeles federal court over the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order barring officials from counting any ballots from the individuals it flagged.The Justice Department filed the lawsuit on October 15, a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before an election.California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data" and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters.California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state.Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.Trump has repeatedly insisted that states are not doing enough to stop voting by noncitizens, which he says is widespread despite multiple studies and state audits showing it is rare.APPEALS COURT REJECTED EMERGENCY REQUESTThe hearing comes after a federal appeals court on Monday rejected an unusual emergency request by the Justice Department asking the appeals court to temporarily block California from counting the ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.The Justice Department did not indicate how many of the more than 20,000 people it flagged in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.Apart from California, the Trump administration has sought to intervene in elections in two states that are home to competitive races.In Alaska, the Justice Department last week asked a judge to prevent certification of election results if the Republican incumbent senator loses by a slim margin, alleging that the presence of another candidate with a similar name on the ballot could confuse voters. Alaska has urged that the case be dismissed, arguing it has taken steps to distinguish the two candidates on the ballot.In Washington state, the Justice Department on Monday sent a letter asking officials not to count any ballots received from 400 voters it said may not be citizens. Washington's top elections official said the timing of the request indicated it was intended to cast unfounded suspicion on election results.California had 23 million registered voters as of December 2025, while Washington had 5 million registered voters as of 2024, state records show.Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the federal government's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizen voters risk wrongly flagging naturalized citizens for removal from the rolls. REUTERS

sources.headline: Lawsuit seeks to block Trump administration effort to find noncitizen voters - Reuters
